📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, have Paris Saint-Germain been defanged? It is too soon to say if injuries have laid low the Champions League's biggest beast, but on the evidence of Wednesday's 2-2 draw with Roma, there might not be quite the same fear factor when opponents find themselves face to face with the kings of Europe's jungle.

Without Khvicha Kvaratskhelia and Desire Doue, both of whom are expected to miss most, if not all, of this season with knee injuries, there simply was not the final-third threat in PSG's ranks to keep Roma honest without the ball. That was all the more pronounced given that Ousmane Dembele was left on the bench until the penalty with which PSG took a 2-1 lead. Maghnes Akliouche, Senny Mayulu and Ferran Torres are talented forwards, the last good enough to win a World Cup final for Spain. Pair one or even two of them with the potential Ballon d'Or winners who started for PSG in the Champions League final, and the drop-off is not particularly significant.

According to recent reports, of course, it might be that Luis Enrique is not particularly minded to see how good his reserves could be flanking Dembele. It would make sense. The Frenchman's fitness needs careful managing at the best of times. With PSG having won their first four league-phase games, there was no pressing need to load up minutes on a player who will surely be needed in the spring. It was a similar story at the base of PSG's team, Ilia Zabarnyi preferred to Marquinhos, another who does well to hit a dozen games before Christmas. This might be a vision of the months ahead for an injury-addled PSG, but it might just be a team that has never taken the league phase particularly seriously not taking the league phase particularly seriously.

Whatever the longer-term view, on the field this evening, PSG's attack lacked the bite to keep Roma backing off. There is a good chance that any team managed by Gian Piero Gasperini might just go man-to-man whoever the opposition, but the fearlessness with which the Giallorossi hurtled around the Parc des Princes was a sure sign they weren't checking over their shoulder quite as much.

Industry observers note that instead, they felt empowered to push on, center back Mario Hermoso on hand to roll in the opener inside the box after an excellent run by Matias Soule. Again, the caveat to assessing how future opponents might take on PSG is that Hermoso has been box-crashing from defense all through this season. You can't be sure he wouldn't have been in the same spot even if he were marking Doue or Kvaratskhelia.

It has been revealed that what you can know is that Roma's aggression when PSG had the ball in open play was not what cost them. Nuno Mendes' ability to blow by his man created concerns, and Achraf Hakimi got his usual shots and shot assists from advanced positions. They could have beaten Roma, but aside from the fullbacks and a few darts into the area by Joao Neves, there was not much to scare Mile Svilar in the champions' lineup.

Instead, it was familiar failings that cost Roma, who might be a real dark horse for this competition when they can successfully defend a corner. Zabarnyi did not even have to win a duel to turn Mayulu's delivery home, just standing in the space between two white shirts at the near post. PSG's second, from the penalty spot, was a Roma confection too. Wesley could argue that Svilar should have been off his line quicker when Hakimi charged in behind, but did the Brazilian need to put his arms on his man at the exact moment he broke into the box? Wesley was lucky not to get a straight red.

In such favorable positions, prime PSG often blitz their opponents. This time, even with Dembele on the field, they could not get clear. Gasperini had an ace of his own on the bench, Donyell Malen sparking Roma after his introduction. A driving run and cutback from the left had PSG scrambling, Vitinha's arm blocking a shot to hand the visitors a penalty that Malen converted.

It has been revealed that had a third goal come, it would probably have been for Roma, Hermoso blazing over late on. There was something more in this for Roma, who remain outside the top 24 despite such impressive displays against Real Madrid, Manchester United and now the holders. As for PSG, there will be time for Luis Enrique to work out how his side dominates Europe with its attack so limited. It would appear there is work to do.

The part-timers who won three Wembley finals in a row

💡 Key Takeaways

  • You probably knew Pep Guardiola's Manchester City won three League Cups on the bounce between 2018 and 2020 before adding a fourth in 2021 â but another side did the silverware hat-trick first.
  • Whitley Bay, who play in the ninth-tier Northern Football League, won three successive FA Vase finals between 2009 and 2011 â an unprecedented achievement in non-league football.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Question: Which two men's club sides have won three successive competition finals at the new Wembley?

You probably knew Pep Guardiola's Manchester City won three League Cups on the bounce between 2018 and 2020 before adding a fourth in 2021 â but another side did the silverware hat-trick first.

Whitley Bay, who play in the ninth-tier Northern Football League, won three successive FA Vase finals between 2009 and 2011 â an unprecedented achievement in non-league football.

The FA Vase, a national competition for amateur teams, was established in 1974; and in more than half a century The Seahorses are the only ones to win it four times â including those three on the trot.

And they did so under the eye of an unassuming IT manager from Sunderland, who used "quiet moments in the day" to strategy historic cup success.

Ian Chandler, who had three spells at Whitley Bay as a player, became manager in 2004 and spent 10 years in charge.

It was no mean feat, as any non-league manager will tell you. Instead of focusing on work meetings, Chandler says he spent more time sorting hotel bookings or discussing scouting reports.

In a recent development, his team were inspired by missing out on Wembley in 2007-08, when Whitley Bay reached the FA Vase semi-finals. They lost 4-0 to Lowestoft Town in the first leg, and despite going 3-0 up inside 20 minutes of the return fixture at Bay's Hillheads Park stadium they were unable to overturn the deficit.

After that elimination, Chandler developed a superstition of never again giving pre-match interviews - as the last time he did so was before the 4-0 defeat.

Whether because of his renewed focus, or because of a desire among players to make amends, it steeled the group to make history.

"It's the hardest thing to keep a team together - as soon as players get noticed, they get picked up at higher level," Chandler tells BBC Sport.

"But after we got to the Vase semis, players wanted to stay and prove what they could do.

"Then the lads wanted to do it again.".

Ian Chandler played for Barnsley, Stockport and Aldershot before a successful non-league career.

Despite being a lifelong Sunderland fan, Chandler admits basing his team on Kevin Keegan's Newcastle - with entertainment even placed above winning.

In a recent development, "There was a standing joke in the team, two or three at the back? One time we chased a game with two at the back," he notes.

"The Premier League can be so boring; fans want to be entertained, that's what we promised.".

Chandler was already a Whitley Bay hero when he was appointed manager by chairman Paul McIlduff, having scored the winner in the 2002 FA Vase final against Tiptree United at Villa Park.

After a slow start as the then-35-year-old with no prior managerial experience found his bearings, Chandler built a talented team which became the envy of non-league football nationwide.

"We played good football. We had pace on the wing, fantastic midfielders, and strikers who were deadly," says McIlduff, who has been Whitley Bay chairman since 2001.

In a recent development, "When we brought them in, it was about fitting the psychology of the dressing room. No-one thought they were better than anyone else, they played for each other.".

A growing influence in the side was the 'Whitley Bay Maradona'.

Paul Robinson came through Newcastle United's academy before a career spent across various non-league clubs in the north-east â including Whitley Bay from 2007 to 2013.

Like several other players and staff, he worked with Chandler both in his day job at software manufacturer Sage and at Hillheads Park.

According to recent reports, "He was my manager at work and football, I was sick of him," he tells BBC Sport. "But it helped get time off for matches.".

And it meant he also had an understanding boss if his mind drifted at work.

"Zoning out happened regularly, picturing scoring and winning, what the opposition would be like - hoping they were rubbish so we could have an easy stroll," he indicates.

Perhaps Robinson's greatest Whitley Bay moment came in the 2010 FA Vase semi-final second leg, when his last-minute diving header in the driving rain secured a 6-5 aggregate victory over Barwell, sparking a pitch invasion.

"Everyone goes to the finals, you were there, you could enjoy it," states Robinson, who is now academy head at South Shields.

It has been revealed that "But the rounds before were the bigger games. At home, we would get 2,000 or 3,000 at every game. You felt like a real player. You associate those memories with 90s FA Cup you never think it will happen in non-league.".

Chandler played in a 2-0 win over Preston in round two as they reached the FA Cup third round for the first and only time in the 1989-90 season, and they also progressed to round two the following campaign.

Those seasons of success - made The Bay a feared side for non-league clubs across England, and meant they were ready for the significant games in a way most amateur sides are not.

"One quarter-final against Biggleswade [in 2009], they turned up in suits and ties," states Robinson. "We thought, this is their day out, their cup final. We won 5-2.

Industry observers note that "By the end, teams were turning up afraid of us. We had it won beforehand.".

Paul Robinson scored the fifth goal in Whitley Bay's 6-1 win over Wroxham in the 2010 FA Vase final.

Off the pitch, the team's success had an influence on the whole of Whitley Bay. A working-class town near Newcastle, which had its heyday as a Victorian-era holiday destination, sporting success brought local pride to the north-east coast.

And like any lower league club, that success could only be supported by dedicated volunteers, who went into overdrive before the Vase finals.

In a recent development, they would go door to door across shops in Tynemouth, North Shields and Whitley Bay to raise support. A van selling tickets was parked outside Woolworths on the high street.

"There was such excitement around the whole of Whitley Bay - every shop had things in the windows, the blue and white stripes," says one of the volunteers, Jenn Robinson.

She got involved because her late husband Mike was a club board member and if she wanted to see him she "had to go around there".

"Everyone wanted to come and watch, we got so many local sponsors," adds Jenn.

Industry observers note that "I still do buffets and things for players and long-standing fans. We have a game tonight, and I'm making the sandwiches now.".

Newcastle United helped out with selling tickets for the finals, while North Tyneside Council provided security services as thousands flocked to Hillheads Park for big cup games.

But even the best laid plans can go awry.

"We organised a train down to London, the guarantee was that it would go straight to Wembley," says McIlduff. "The first time it worked, second time they were taken to Kings Cross - we had to organise taxis up to Wembley.".

By hook or by crook, The Seahorses army made it three times to the national stadium. Some even got royal treatment.

"It was absolutely surreal, and a delight," Jenn says. "The first Wembley final we played at, it had just opened. My husband being on the board, we sat in the royal box, which was fabulous.

Recent findings suggest that "One of the security guys showing me to our seats stated, 'Miss Robinson, this is Prince William's seat'. He hadn't even sat in it at that point.".

Thousands of fans travelled from Whitley Bay to London across the three finals.

Chandler, whose son Benjamin was a mascot at all three finals, noted it was an overwhelming experience at times for the players too.

Recent findings suggest that "The first year was crazy, everything was brand newly introduced," he notes. "The first year the bus driver scraped the side up of the bus driving into the ground.

"The second year we tried to take everything in, all the lads had their mobiles. Then the third year, it was just a case of can we do it, win three in a row.".

And three times, Whitley Bay rose to the occasion.

After beating Glossop North End 2-0 in 2009 in front of 12,200 supporters, Whitley Bay returned a year later to thrash Wroxham 6-1.

According to recent reports, the opening goal was scored by prolific striker Paul Chow after only 21 seconds. At the time this was the quickest goal in a Wembley final and was only surpassed 13 years later when Ilkay Gundogan scored for Manchester City inside 13 seconds in the FA Cup final.

The hat-trick was completed in 2011 with a frantic 3-2 win over Coalville Town, who equalised twice before Chow was again the hero with an 86th-minute winner.

In total, nearly 30,000 fans were in the stands across the three finals.

After each final, Whitley Bay celebrated in The Green Man pub just 15 minutes' walk from the famous Wembley arch.

Recent findings suggest that "In the first year we just went back to the bar and it was an anti-climax," Robinson says. "The second and third years the club got their act together and we rented a room; families, friends and fans were invited, they were brilliant nights.

"In 2010, we actually spent 10 days together - the week of the final we spent as a squad preparing, then we went to Marbella for five nights. Best 10 days of my life!".

In a recent development, the 2010 trophy lift was perhaps the most emotional though, as the players were joined by former team-mate Mark Taylor. He had played in the previous year's final, before being diagnosed with motor neurone disease, forcing an early retirement.

Recent findings suggest that "Mark used to come on the away trips after he got diagnosed, he just wanted to be Mark - we had a good laugh everywhere we went," indicates Chandler. "He's still knocking about, abusing me on Facebook. He was the core of our second and third year.".

Whitley Bay lift the trophy in 2010, joined by former team-mate Mark Taylor (left).

Sources indicate that success ensured the lives of Chandler and his team were never quite the same again. Reporters turned up to Sage to speak with the manager and his players; even Chandler's mum was interviewed by BBC Radio Newcastle legend Paul Dixon.

Chandler - and his wife - even got up close and personal with managerial icons.

"I was invited to the annual sports awards in Manchester. There were people there like Sven Goran Eriksson and Sir Alex Ferguson [and] numerous others," he indicates.

"I had my wife with me and Sven came over gave her a peck on the cheek - she wasn't aware of who it was until I told her later that evening.".

Robinson admitted that going back to work at an IT company after Wembley glory was a "massive comedown".

"One year I got a standing ovation when I walked into the office, but after that it was just back to normal," he indicates.

Recent findings suggest that "People wind you up about it - 'are you talking about Wembley again? Give it a rest Robbo!".

Like all good things, Whitley Bay's golden era came to an end. Chandler departed in 2014 after a dip in form; the club have not won a major honour since the 2011 FA Vase and remain in the ninth tier.

But the memories in the football-mad north-east remain.

"Me and my wife went out on a Sunday at a pub in Durham just a few weeks back, and this guy came up out the blue and asked, 'Are you Ian Chandler?'" he laughs.

Industry observers note that "Then he started talking about that team; in the north-east, everyone follows football. It was so lovely.".

#208774. Back to 1997: Russia wants NATO to roll back its eastern expansion

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1093 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dw ↗ Open Full Page

Back to 1997: Russia wants NATO to roll back its eastern expansion

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1093 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • During talks on ending the war in Ukraine, Russian representatives in Abu Dhabi presented a document containing far-reaching demands, The Newly introduced York Times reports.
  • Dated November 10, the document reportedly calls not only for an end to Western arms deliveries to Ukraine but also for NATO to withdraw its troops and bases and move them back to where they were in 1997.
  • The year 1997 refers to the NATO alliance before its first eastward expansion, according to the Kremlin.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

During talks on ending the war in Ukraine, Russian representatives in Abu Dhabi presented a document containing far-reaching demands, The Newly introduced York Times reports.

Dated November 10, the document reportedly calls not only for an end to Western arms deliveries to Ukraine but also for NATO to withdraw its troops and bases and move them back to where they were in 1997.

The year 1997 refers to the NATO alliance before its first eastward expansion, according to the Kremlin. At the time, NATO had 16 members. Poland, the Czech Republic and Hungary had already been invited to join but did not formally become members of the defense alliance until two years later. In the following years, more countries in Central, Eastern and Southeastern Europe joined, followed most recently by countries in Scandinavia. Today, NATO has 32 member states in Europe and North America.

According to the report, Russia is not explicitly demanding that Central and Eastern European countries leave, but rather that the NATO alliance end its military presence in those countries.

A withdrawal of NATO troops and bases from member states that joined the alliance after 1997 would significantly weaken their defense capabilities. For example, since 2004, NATO allies, including Germany, have taken turns policing the airspace over Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania.

Industry observers note that because the Baltic states do not have fighter jets of their own for independent air policing, NATO provides the capability. Since 2026, the mission has been part of a broader air defense presence. The planned deployment of the German Lithuania Brigade, which is expected to be fully operational by the end of 2027, would also have to be halted.

According to recent reports, in Romania, meanwhile, the Mihail Kogalniceanu Air Base near Constanța on the Black Sea is right now being expanded. Once completed, it is set to become Europe's largest NATO air base by area — even larger than Ramstein in Germany.

It has been revealed that "Under no circumstances will we allow anyone to establish latest security rules for this part of the world over the heads of Poland and Europe," Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk told TVP World. His Bulgarian counterpart, Rumen Radev, called a NATO withdrawal "unthinkable and unrealistic." No country should be forced by external pressure to reverse its decision on which alliance to join.

Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal also rejected any Russian say in changes to Europe's security order: "We have nothing to discuss with Russia about Europe's security order; it is working well.".

The strong rejection from the capitals of NATO's eastern members, however, masks fears along the alliance's eastern flank that a deal between Washington and Moscow could turn their security into a bargaining chip.

In the event of an armed attack on a NATO member, the other alliance members are obligated under Article 5 to come to its aid. Each member decides for itself what measures it considers necessary, which may include the use of military force.

According to recent reports, for the mutual defense commitment to deter a potential aggressor, that country must believe NATO can intervene militarily quickly and effectively in a crisis. The deployment of allied troops along the eastern flank serves precisely this purpose. A withdrawal would make defense more difficult and could lead Russia to believe that an attack on NATO territory would involve fewer risks for Moscow.

As part of their security framework, European countries have agreed that states are free to decide which alliances they wish to join. NATO points to Article 10 of its founding treaty, which enshrines its open-door policy for European countries. The 1997 NATO-Russia Founding Act also explicitly stated that neither side had the right to veto the other's decisions.

Back in November 1990, the participating states of the Conference on Security and Cooperation in Europe (CSCE), including the Soviet Union, had already agreed in the Charter of Paris to respect each country's freedom to choose its own security arrangements.

During the negotiations surrounding German reunification, then-US Secretary of State James Baker and German Foreign Minister Hans-Dietrich Genscher used language that suggested putting limits on NATO's eastward expansion.

Industry observers note that their remarks came during discussions about unified Germany's membership in NATO and the possible deployment of NATO forces on the territory of the former East Germany. However, no written, legally binding general promise was ever agreed that NATO would never expand to include other former Warsaw Pact countries.

Industry observers note that in the 1997 NATO-Russia Founding Act, both sides declared that they no longer considered each other adversaries. NATO stated that, under the security conditions prevailing at the time and in the foreseeable future, it intended to ensure its collective defense through reinforcement rather than the additional permanent stationing of "substantial combat forces." The agreement explicitly gave Moscow no veto over NATO decisions.

In the 1994 Budapest Memorandum, Russia, the United States and the United Kingdom reaffirmed their commitment to respect Ukraine's independence and existing borders and to refrain from the use of force. These assurances were linked to Ukraine's decision to give up its nuclear weapons. However, the memorandum did not oblige the United States or the United Kingdom to defend Ukraine militarily in the event of an attack. NATO membership was not addressed at the time.

Industry observers note that just over two months before Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, the Kremlin presented two draft treaties to the United States and NATO. In them, Russia demanded an end to further NATO enlargement. The draft agreement with NATO also proposed that Russia and NATO members that had already joined the alliance as of May 27, 1997, refrain from deploying additional troops or weapons on the territory of other European countries beyond the levels stationed there on that date.

According to recent reports, security guarantees for the postwar period and a future security framework for Europe were also on the agenda in Abu Dhabi. Negotiating NATO troop deployments and alliance enlargement alongside an end to the war in Ukraine would give Moscow additional leverage. Russia has long maintained that the "root causes" of the war must be addressed. The Kremlin includes NATO enlargement and the alliance's military presence in Eastern Europe among those causes.

According to recent reports, so far, no significant Western player has expressed willingness to accept Russia's demands in Abu Dhabi. On the contrary, former Polish intelligence coordinator Stanislaw Zaryn viewed the talks as an attempt to buy time and weaken the West ahead of another confrontation.

The Unpromotables: Germany's league champions who can't go up

📅 02 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1791 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Djamal Ziane is a three-time league champion â but he does not always feel like it.
  • This summer, for the second year in a row and for the third time in seven seasons, the Lokomotive Leipzig captain hoisted the trophy into the air having led his team to the title in the Regional League Northeast, the fourth tier of German football.
  • But the memory is tinged with frustration because, just as in 2025 and 2020, Lokomotive's league title did not lead to promotion.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Djamal Ziane is a three-time league champion â but he does not always feel like it.

This summer, for the second year in a row and for the third time in seven seasons, the Lokomotive Leipzig captain hoisted the trophy into the air having led his team to the title in the Regional League Northeast, the fourth tier of German football.

But the memory is tinged with frustration because, just as in 2025 and 2020, Lokomotive's league title did not lead to promotion.

In a recent development, while the other regional champions in the German fourth division were promoted to the nationwide 3. Liga, "Lok" faced a play-off against a representative of the Regional League Bavaria, Wurzburger Kickers. Ziane scored, but an injury-ravaged Leipzig lost 3-1 on aggregate.

"Euer System ist krank," read a simple protest banner displayed by the 2,000 travelling supporters â "your system is sick".

"It's the worst thing â injury aside â that you can experience as a footballer," Ziane tells BBC Sport.

Sources indicate that "Catastrophe doesn't cut it. It doesn't make any sense. If they really wanted to change it, they could do tomorrow.".

A banner reading 'Your system is sick' was displayed at this year's promotion play-off.

Germany's football pyramid has a bottleneck.

Beneath the Bundesliga, 2. Bundesliga and 3. Liga, the fourth tier is split into five regional divisions (North, West, Southwest, Northeast and Bavaria), each of which produces a league champion.

In a recent development, so far, so good. But with only four teams being relegated from the 3. Liga each season, the sums don't add up.

Sources indicate that an unsatisfactory solution is currently in place: the champions in the West and Southwest go up automatically while a third automatic promotion spot is rotated among the other three leagues in a three-year cycle. The fourth spot is allocated via a play-off between the winners of the remaining two leagues.

One champion always misses out and, increasingly, it's the champion from the Regional League Northeast, covering the territory of the former eastern German Democratic Republic (GDR).

Recent findings suggest that in addition to Lok Leipzig's triple tragedy, former serial GDR Oberliga winners Dynamo Berlin fell short in 2022 and Energie Cottbus drew the short straw in 2023. This season, there is only one eastern German club in the 3. Liga: Hansa Rostock.

The struggles of the regions' football clubs are, to some degree, a result of continuing socio-economic disparities between east and west, which were also reflected in the success of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party in recent state elections.

According to recent reports, even in 2026, not one of the 40 leading companies listed on Germany's DAX stock exchange is based in the former east (outside Berlin). Salaries remain lower, unemployment remains higher and the population is older and shrinking as young people move west.

The reason that automatic promotion spots are handed to the champions in the West and Southwest is simply because there are more men's football teams registered in those jurisdictions - because more people live there.

It is an argument that Ziane is tired of hearing.

"In that case, you might as well give us the automatic promotion spot because we attract bigger crowds," he states.

It has been revealed that indeed, the average attendance in the Regional League Northeast last season (3,125) was around twice as high as that in the other leagues. Lok Leipzig themselves had the fourth highest (6,352). More than 11,000 attended the local derby against city rivals Chemie Leipzig.

"Unfortunately, you don't get any points for tradition, crowds and history," indicates 39-year-old Lok chief executive Toni Wachsmuth, who does not have access to sponsors with the same financial firepower as his counterparts further west.

"The [western] leagues do have better economic foundations but everyone agrees that the current system is nonsense. Everyone needs to compromise but some officials are clearly putting their own interests and positions above the general good of German football.".

It comes as little surprise, therefore, that the latest push for change has come from the east, with clubs launching a latest campaign in March 2025 with the slogan: "Meister mussen aufsteigen!" â champions must go up!

Their proposal: a reduction from five leagues to four, with the precise geographical borders to be determined anew each season with the help of artificial intelligence, taking into account factors such as distance of travel to away games and attractive derbies.

Recent findings suggest that they call it the compass model. Because it can go in all directions. In return, the Regional League Northeast is prepared to compromise by giving up its emotional attachment to the territory of the former East Germany.

In a recent development, "I want to get away from this east-west debate," indicates Tommy Haeder, the 35-year-old chief executive of Chemnitzer FC and figurehead of the reform campaign. "We've had a change of generation. Many older officials have retired and been replaced by younger people who don't have this nostalgia for the GDR.".

Haeder also emphasises the benefits that a fairer promotion system would bring for German football as a whole, arguing that eastern clubs would be better equipped to continue nurturing youth talent.

"It's not in the interest of talent development when young footballers from Chemnitz are torn away from their homes and families at the age of 10 to join academies in Hamburg, Dortmund or Stuttgart," he tells BBC Sport.

Recent findings suggest that "The compass model is a model in which every region sacrifices a little bit to solve a much bigger problem. We're organised, we have a blueprint, we've made suggestions. Now it's up to the federations to act.".

The campaign has since gained the support of more than 80 clubs across Germany, from east to west and up and down the pyramid.

Union Berlin, who were playing in the fourth tier as recently as the 2000s, became the first Bundesliga club to officially back the initiative, with club president Dirk Zingler saying: "The current set-up contradicts our understanding of sporting competition.".

Borussia Dortmund president â and Bundesliga chairman â Hans-Joachim Watzke added his influential voice, stating: "Champions must go up and we think the compass model with four regional leagues is the best option.".

According to recent reports, support also has also come from Bournemouth head coach Marco Rose who, drawing on his past as both a player and coach at Lok Leipzig, said: "I know what it's like for clubs trying to work within their means, or lack of means, at that level. Everything is on a knife edge.

"You have to give the clubs and their fans the belief that their efforts and sacrifices will be rewarded with promotion.".

Momentum was growing before a key vote at the end of June when, after months of discussions, clubs were finally set to vote on the compass model â but the ballot descended into farce when, at the last minute, the regional federations conducting the vote unveiled two key changes:.

Suddenly, the four new leagues would consist of only 18 teams rather than 20 (thus making the compass model less attractive because 10 more teams would miss out), and a stipulation was added that a majority be reached in each of the five regions for the model to pass.

An overall majority (50.9%) in favour of the compass model was still reached (including 60.9% in the West, 61.5% in the North and 76.3% in the Northeast) but the Southwest voted for an alternative option in which the northeastern league would be dissolved and its clubs reallocated, while the Southwest and West would simply remain the same.

"The move from a functioning system to a complex, insecure and economically riskier model without an obvious benefit doesn't make any sense to me," Robert Lempka, chief executive of Regional League Southwest side FSV Frankfurt told local public broadcaster Hessischer Rundfunk this summer. "I find it unsettling that an untransparent algorithm should decide a club's future.".

Recent findings suggest that the Bavarians, meanwhile, voted vaguely for "further talks", with Bavarian Football Federation (BFV) President Christoph Kern telling Munich's Abendzeitung newspaper in August: "We've gathered our clubs together on several occasions and none of the suggested models have majority support. I'm not prepared to simply give up the Regional League Bavaria like that.".

According to recent reports, for Haeder in Chemnitz, the vote was "an absolute catastrophe â completely amateurish". And he's not alone.

This season, protests have erupted across German football. In the Regional League Northeast, almost every game has begun with a delay as players have simply refused to play for the first minute.

On the opening day, Lok Leipzig supporters, their team still stranded in the same division, threw hundreds of plastic trophies on to the pitch, symbolising the worthlessness of their club's back-to-back titles.

Down in Bavaria, Bayern Munich's ultras attended a reserve team game in the regional league and produced an intricate choreography criticising the Bavarian Football Federation (BFV) for what they perceive to be an unco-operative stance.

"You've taken us for fools long enough," read a banner beneath a display depicting BFV officials using a magnet to pull a compass needle towards them. The ultras then set off red pyrotechnics which turned the compass needle back in the direction of the fans.

Sources indicate that and before the international break, fans of clubs across the Bundesliga used their platform to call for reform with co-ordinated banners reading: "Clubs and fans betrayed! Champions must go up! Compass model now!".

The compass, it would appear, may finally be pointing towards a resolution after the German Football Federation (DFB) confirmed the convening of an extraordinary general meeting on 18 December.

Recent findings suggest that "[The issue] must be resolved," noted President Bernd Neuendorf. "The compass model received the most votes and offers the best chance for a concentration of elite performance and therefore better development of talent.".

Sources indicate that any changes would only be implemented in the 2028-29 season â too late for Ziane who, now 34, has embarked on his 13th season with Lok Leipzig. Back-to-back champions, but still in the fourth division.

"You can never completely get over it because, at our level, the 3. Liga is probably the pinnacle. Promotion with my hometown club would have been the most wonderful thing in the world for me," he indicates before heading out for training.

"It's a shame that we have to force ourselves to remember what we've achieved. It's so hard to win this league and we did it twice in a row! You can't take that for granted.".

The part-timers who won three Wembley finals in a row.

Are women better than men at endurance running?

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that there are two non-negotiables for Chelsea managers. Do not lose at home to Tottenham Hotspur and do not lose at home to Leeds United. But Xabi Alonso has now completed the nightmare double.

Just as Spurs broke their Stamford Bridge hoodoo a few weeks ago, Leeds secured their first win at Chelsea since 1999 by humiliating the hosts after falling a goal behind.

It was 67 long years since Chelsea had last lost at home to Tottenham and Leeds in the same season, and Alonso was left in no doubt about how seriously supporters take that as his team were loudly booed and he was heckled.

Cole Palmer stormed down the tunnel at full time, ignoring the advice of Chelsea’s so-called “cultural architect” Willie Isa to applaud the remaining home fans, and shrugging off the attention of injured striker João Pedro.

Having been left out of the last England squad, Palmer was largely anonymous for Chelsea but he was not alone and Alonso is already facing similar questions to his predecessors about the team’s mentality.

Sources indicate that “I felt that probably we are in a fragile moment, mentally,” Alonso said. “When we receive a punch, we didn’t recover that strong, that tough enough and today that was my feeling.

“The fans were disappointed because the expectations from them are high and we feel sorry for them. For sure, it’s not the easiest moment. It’s a fragile moment, but we need to work together and stick together because there is still a long way to go.”.

Alonso is yet to name the same starting XI for successive league games and there appears to be no discernible plan or style of play.

Injuries have contributed to Chelsea’s unremarkable start to the season under Alonso – and Moisés Caicedo was forced off early in the first half – but the problems run deeper than the treatment table.

According to recent reports, alonso’s defence has now conceded 20 goals, which has contributed to Chelsea losing five league games already – more than Manchester United. In between three defeats in their last four league games, Chelsea were also knocked out of the Carabao Cup.

In a recent development, the Spaniard had answered questions about Chelsea’s identity, or lack of it, by saying he wanted his team to be competitive. But they were anything but against a Leeds side who had seven more shots than their hosts and five more on target.

It is hard to fathom how, through all the chopping and changing, Wesley Fofana still starts games for Chelsea in defence. It was his pathetic attempted header, which bounced backwards towards his own goal, that contributed to Noah Okafor’s first goal.

Josh Acheampong also got himself into a mess and Okafor was somehow able to squeeze a shot past goalkeeper Emi Martínez despite having three Chelsea players around him.

Chelsea had taken the lead through striker Emmanuel Emegha, on his first start for the club, but from that moment on they were second best with Leeds pair Ethan Ampadu and Ao Tanaka running the middle of the park.

Dominic Calvert-Lewin had hit the crossbar and failed to find the net with three more presentable opportunities in the first half, but he took his chance from the penalty spot eight minutes after the break.

Morgan Rogers had argued that James Justin’s shot hit him too far up his arm for it to be a penalty, but a VAR check upheld referee Michael Oliver’s decision and Calvert-Lewin kept his cool.

That should have been the moment that shook Chelsea into action and prompted a response but, instead, Alonso’s team fell apart and he was unable to provoke a shift in momentum from the touchline.

Just five minutes after Calvert-Lewin had put Leeds ahead, Okafor effectively sealed the victory by firing the ball into the net after Chelsea had failed to deal with a long throw into their penalty area.

Noah Okafor's brace helps seal Leeds' first Premier League win at Stamford Bridge since 1999! 💥 https://t.co/UAmsJziJmZ.

“I can’t wait to be on the sofa with coffee and cake and also watch this game back because it was a really good game,” Daniel Farke, the Leeds head coach, stated. “I was a bit disappointed even at half-time when it was just a draw, because I think we were the better side from the first to the last.”.

According to recent reports, john Terry still works with Chelsea’s academy and it might be worth Alonso getting the former captain to speak to the club’s senior players about how to defend and compete. Whatever has been done on the training pitch so far has not worked.

Alonso’s substitutes are yet to register a single goal or assist in the league this season and his changes failed to make any sort of impact here. For the visitors, however, two substitutes combined to score their fourth goal in time added on for stoppages.

Harry Wilson played in Brenden Aaronson and, from a tight angle, he managed to find the back of the net by sending the ball through the legs of Martínez.

The home stands were already half-empty by that point, but some supporters hung around to show their displeasure and Palmer could not contain his anger.

We know what the history of this game is like and what the fans expect - we know they have wanted a win here for a long time. It’s right we can enjoy this performance.

According to recent reports, frank’s start to life at Palace begins with defeat but an improved display. Coventry are up to 13th with their fourth win of the season.

Another home win for Tottenham, who managed the game well and introduced a new star to the Premier League in Williams-Barnett.

Industry observers note that what a day for Leeds. They scored four and it could have been more. For Chelsea, they lost their way when Caicedo went off and without Joao Pedro, they have lost their spark in attack.

Bournemouth make it nine wins in a row in all competitions after doing enough in the first half to get the job done.

Leeds finish the match in style as Aaronson puts the seal on an impressive away day.

It’s all over and Sunderland deservedly leave with a point. Villa will be very disappointed by their display.

It has been revealed that what was I saying in the last post?! The home side are on the attack Thomas-Asante pokes a shot at goal and forces Henderson into a save but hits his own player McNeil, who bundles the ball in the net.

It has been revealed that can Chelsea stage a late fightback? Will we get a winner between Coventry and Palace?

Needing a goal, Emery makes a bold decision to take off Villa’s top scorer and bring on Madjo.

Despite the two-goal lead and the magnificent debut performance of Luca Williams-Barnett, the home support has remained subdued throughout the afternoon.

At times, the shouts of two children sat just behind the press box feel like by far the loudest noise in the stadium - although that might just be proximity.

Much quieter half at the CBS Arena but Palace are more likely to get a third goal.

It has been revealed that this has gone from bad to worse for Chelsea. One supporter near the dug-outs was so angry at Leeds scoring a third goal that he got up and screamed his displeasure at manager Xabi Alonso.

1999 was the last time Leeds won at Chelsea. Today looks like they will get another, as Okafor takes advantage of more poor defending to finish past Martinez.

Villa’s fans are now chanting loudly for substitute John McGinn to be introduced.

They are getting their wish, too, as the Scotland international is coming on with winger Ibrahim Mbaye.

Villa need an injection of energy.

Morgan Rogers and Chelsea are pretty upset about that penalty being awarded to Leeds. They felt the ball struck him too far up his arm to be a penalty. Calvert-Lewin took his spot-kick superbly and it’s gone very, very quiet among the home fans.

It has been revealed that everything Luca Williams-Barnett touches is turning to gold today. He has a goal to his name already, and adds an assist just six minutes into the second half.

From almost the halfway line, he drove forward, weaving his way expertly into the box before picking out Dominic Solanke in the middle of the box, who tapped the ball into the back of the net.

However, the atmosphere is still a touch subdued, despite James Maddison urging the crowd to make themselves heard almost immediately after the goal, the noise drops to almost a murmur.

In a recent development, rogers blocks Bogle’s drive with his arm and Michael Oliver gives a penalty to Leeds. After a long check, VAR confirms it.

Williams-Barnet gets one-on-one with Furlong and gets past him with ease before firing a cross for Solanke to finish.

Thomas Frank declared “it’s good to be back in the circus” of football management ahead of his first match as Crystal Palace boss.

The 53-year-old Dane admitted he could have easily spent a few more months sipping wine, “eating too well” and collecting passport stamps, but something resonated when he asked his wife why he was tempted to seek out a upcoming job and she told him, “(It’s) because you can’t help yourself”.

Frank hinted that there was more behind the story to his disappointing spell at Tottenham he might one day reveal, but for now he has a team to rescue from a relegation fight, beginning with today’s trip to Coventry.

If you don’t learn from any of your jobs, I don’t think you reflect, I don’t think you improve, and I don’t think you get better.

Industry observers note that of course there’s a lot of things I have been reflecting over. The details, that will be for another time, but I can say I’ve learned, definitely.

I was very aware I didn’t want to do anything in the summer. I put a statement out there, I needed more time. I can actually, honestly say I would have been fine if it was three, four, five, six, seven months more, because it’s good to be back in the circus, but it’s also unbelievably good not to be in, especially if you enjoy life, which I do.

I was spending time with family and friends and doing all that, but I think the club, the way Palace is, how well Steve Parish especially spoke about the club and ideas, Matt Hobbs and Iain Moody and these guys, too, helped convince me it was a good idea.

Tottenham’s impressive run of form came to a crashing halt with a 1-0 defeat to Leeds just before the international break, but manager Roberto De Zerbi will be hoping for a fresh start - even if he will not be pitchside after picking up a second yellow card of the season.

De Zerbi made six changes from the aforementioned defeat to Leeds, including a first start for teenager Luca Williams-Barnett, a player who has come through the club’s academy.

There is no place in the squad for Sandro Tonali or Tosin Adarabioyo, but James Maddison will start for the first time since the 2-0 defeat to Chelsea in October.

Aston Villa 2.0 was always likely to be a slow-burner, and it is proving exactly that for Unai Emery.

His team has impressed and underwhelmed in equal measure so far this season but this is an opportunity to hoist themselves up the table.

A clean sheet would be a good starting point, as they have not secured a shutout in front of their own fans in the league since March.

Good afternoon and welcome to coverage from the Premier League as domestic football returns after an international break.

We have five matches to bring you, including Chelsea vs Leeds, Aston Villa vs Sunderland and Tottenham vs Ipswich.

Xabi Alonso remarked his Chelsea side needs to learn to deal with the absence of Joao Pedro as the Blues struggle for goals in the absence of their injured striker.

The Brazilian has not played since the 2-0 win over Everton on October 17 and will be unavailable again today.

Without a focal point in the number nine position, Chelsea’s goal output has been dramatically reduced and they have dropped to fifth and having suffered two defeats in their last three games.

“(We need) the whole team for that,” mentioned Alonso. “It’s not just the strikers that can score. We can score from set-pieces, from defenders, from midfielders.

“It’s teamwork. For sure Joao is an vital player but we need to deal with this time without him. So far we have tried different options and we need to keep trying.

In a recent development, “We need to deal with it. It’s not that I’m going to look for one explanation. I think that there are more explanations for one defeat than missing just one player.”.

Gary O’Neil is targeting a “special” result at Tottenham, but promised Ipswich will not make any drastic changes after a four-match winless run.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Published: 15:03 EST, 26 November 2026 | Updated: 15:03 EST, 26 November 2026.

Bruno Fernandes and Manchester United were the beneficiaries of a bizarre goal in the Champions League on Wednesday night, as the captain's long-range effort bounced up off the turf and deceived the goalkeeper to help earn Mauricio Pochettino a 2-2 draw with Sporting Lisbon in his second game in charge.

Football has certainly seen its fair share of quirky, bizarre and downright bonkers goals over the years, and Fernandes' effort in Lisbon is certainly one to add to the collection.

Here, Daily Mail Sport's reporters look back at some of the strangest goals they can remember, from outrageous goalkeeping blunders to freakish deflections and moments of sheer misfortune.

Darren Bent (Sunderland 1-0 Liverpool) - October 17, 2009.

Sources indicate that forget bouncing in off a divot, try the ball flying into the net off a beach ball. Darren Bent’s winner against Liverpool at the Stadium of Light back in 2009 has got to be the strangest.

A Liverpool fan lobbed a gigantic red beach ball on to the pitch (in the middle of October) which was initially removed by a steward only for the wind to blow it back.

What made it even funnier was that when Bent’s shot struck it, Liverpool keeper Pepe Reina tried to save the inflatable, which now resides in the National Football Museum, instead of the actual ball that flew past him.

Thank heavens there was no VAR back then to spoil the day.

Pepe Reina had no chance after Darren Bent's strike ricocheted off a beach ball into the goal.

Peter Enckelman (Birmingham vs Aston Villa) - September 16, 2002.

In a recent development, obviously the mind immediately goes to balloons and players ghosting behind goalkeepers. But my favourite happened on September 16, 2002 between Birmingham City and Aston Villa.

Olof Mellberg took a throw-in. He threw it back to Peter Enckelman. The ball bounced under Enckelman’s foot and rolled into the Villa goal. Referee David Elleray reckoned he must have touched it with his studs.

In a recent development, it was all made worse for Enckelman with a Birmingham fan hopping out of the crowd to goad him to his face. I must have been nine years old and remember watching all this live.

Can’t imagine my parents told me what that hand gesture the fan was doing in front of Enckelman meant.

Peter Enckelman scored a disastrous own goal after the ball bounced underneath his foot.

Mo Diame (Brighton vs Newcastle) - February 28, 2017.

Brighton half cleared a corner and Christian Atsu returned a scuffed volley, which was helped on by the toe of Daryl Murphy, before Mo Diame planted his foot in the ground and allowed the ball to bounce off the back of his heel, looping up and over all inside the goalmouth and into the top corner.

I was there, and I have revisited my match report.

Sources indicate that 'Diame had been stood still for the majority of the previous 81 minutes,' I wrote. 'Finally, it was a tactic which served him well.'.

I also refer to the goal as fluky and hilarious. It is now the stuff of legend on Tyneside, for it helped Newcastle to win promotion as champions. Indeed, without it, Brighton would have finished top and Newcastle second.

Mo Diame scored one of the craziest goals in Championship history against Brighton in 2017.

Tony Popovic (Portsmouth vs Crystal Palace) - September 11, 2004.

It has been revealed that some goals stay with you because of the sublime, others because of the ridiculous. And I doubt I'll ever see a stranger goal live than Tony Popovic's flying backheel into his own net in 2004.

With Portsmouth protecting a 2-1 lead late on against Crystal Palace, nerves were jangling around Fratton Park until Popovic's moment of spectacular misfortune.

Pompey's Steve Stone floated a hopeful cross into the Palace box, prompting Popovic to stretch out a leg in an attempt to clear. Instead, he somehow managed to flick the ball off his boot, onto the post and into the net, producing a finish any top striker would be proud of.

Olivier Giroud, eat your heart out.

Portsmouth couldn't believe their luck when Tony Popovic flicked the ball into in his own net.

Nani (Manchester United vs Tottenham) - October 30, 2010.

This one has always stuck with me, partly for the sheer audacity of Nani and partly because it's the sort of goal that simply wouldn't escape VAR scrutiny today.

Back when a trip to Manchester United was still a fearsome prospect, Spurs were a goal down and chasing a late equaliser when Nani was brought down in the penalty area and appeared to handle the ball.

Recent findings suggest that crucially, though, Mark Clattenburg had not blown his whistle. Tottenham goalkeeper Heurelho Gomes, assuming a free-kick had been awarded, placed the ball on the ground.

Recent findings suggest that still gesticulating, Nani got up, realised the ball was still live, and coolly passed it into the back of the net. Cue bedlam in the Stretford End.

Nani celebrates his controversial goal against Spurs, to the fury of goalkeeper Heurelho Gomes.

Zlatan Ibrahimovic (Sweden vs England) - November 14, 2012.

It's not weird in the category of a divot or a beach ball but the most outlandish goal I've ever seen live was Zlatan Ibrahimovic's 30-yard overhead kick for Sweden against England at the Friends Arena in Stockholm in November 2012.

It has been revealed that A long ball came over the top of the England defence, Joe Hart ran out and headed it clear and Ibrahimovic launched himself into the air, hooking the ball in a majestic arc over England's disbelieving goalkeeper. Great goals can be strange, too.

Zlatan Ibrahimovic's acrobatic bicycle kick against England was both strange and sensational.

Stan Collymore (Blackburn vs Liverpool) - February 24, 1996.

As soon as I watched Fernandes' speculative long-range strike bobble past Sporting Lisbon goalkeeper Kaique Pereira, my mind immediately cast back to Tim Flowers being embarrassed by Stan Collymore at Ewood Park in 1996.

Not that it was the Blackburn goalkeeper's fault, of course. Collymore's feeble effort from distance in the 11th minute trickled along the turf before hitting a rogue divot and bouncing over Flowers' head into the net.

Collymore, who cracked a smile but toned down his celebrations, turned away in disbelief as Flowers stared down at the pitch with his hands on his hips.

Liverpool went on to win the game 3-2 and Flowers described it as 'one of those ridiculous situations'.

Stan Collymore scored one of the strangest goals when his effort bobbled over Tim Flowers.

Gary Neville (England vs Croatia) - October 11, 2006.

Sources indicate that strange bobbles take me back to Gary Neville’s own goal in Zagreb. Early in the doomed England reign of Steve McClaren.

Industry observers note that neville rolled a simple back pass towards Paul Robinson who took a mighty swing at fresh air with his right boot and looked aghast as it trundled past him and into the net for Croatia's second in a 2-0 win. The Spurs keeper stamped furiously at the offending divot as the Maksimir Stadium erupted.

Adding another layer to the comic value were pitchside LED ad screens flashing up images of Sacha Baron Cohen’s latest Borat film and one of his lame catchphrases: 'I like you'.

It was a bad omen at the start of the failed Euro 2008 campaign and the beginning of the end for both Robinson and Neville in England colours.

Gary Neville's own goal against Croatia came after Paul Robinson totally missed the ball.

Stefan Kiessling (Hoffenheim v Leverkusen) - October 18, 2013.

Legendary Bayer Leverkusen forward Stefan Kiessling has got to be one of the only players to score with a shot off target.

While away to Hoffenheim, a corner was swung in towards Leverkusen striker Kiessling, who, at first glance, simply headed home smartly.

But on closer inspection we can see that the ball was destined for the side netting and an inconspicuous hole in the side of the net let the ball slip in.

Even Kiessling himself had his head in his hands thinking he’d missed before turning around to see his teammates were celebrating.

Leverkusen's Stefan Kiessling must be one of the only players to score with a shot off target.

Can smart cities attract the talent they need to thrive?

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2139 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Robots compete in a football event during RoboCup 2026, a robotics and AI competition held at the Songdo Convensia convention centre in Incheon, South Korea.
  • More than half of the world’s population now lives in cities, and that figure is projected to increase to nearly 70% by 2050.
  • Industry observers note that as the global competition for talent and investment intensifies, many governments see these upcoming cities and urban areas as strategic resources for boosting their innovative and economic competitiveness.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Robots compete in a football event during RoboCup 2026, a robotics and AI competition held at the Songdo Convensia convention centre in Incheon, South Korea. Credit: Ahn Young-joon/Associated Press/ALAMY.

More than half of the world’s population now lives in cities, and that figure is projected to increase to nearly 70% by 2050. With the numbers of urban dwellers set to expand rapidly in some regions, a new generation of towns and cities is on the rise: communities that are designed to be cleaner and more efficient, driven by a host of technologies such as artificial intelligence and the Internet of Things — a network of sensors and devices that collect and transmit data about their surroundings.

Industry observers note that as the global competition for talent and investment intensifies, many governments see these upcoming cities and urban areas as strategic resources for boosting their innovative and economic competitiveness. Research facilities, both public and private, are central to this strategy.

Nature Index 2026 Science cities.

Nature Index 2026 Science cities.

In a recent development, in Songdo, South Korea — an early experiment in building a smart city from the ground up — biopharmaceutical giants such as Samsung Biologics have built major manufacturing facilities, and academic institutions such as Yonsei University have set up training and research centres to nurture scientists. In Hengqin, a rapidly developing district in the Pearl River Delta of southern China, research institutions also play a key role in a government strategy aimed at attracting talent, diversifying the economy and building a reputation for high-tech innovation.

It has been revealed that for some researchers, purpose-built tech-centric cities provide them with the ideal environment to conduct experiments. Air-quality and traffic-flow research benefits greatly from consistent, real-time data gathered from many different locations, for instance. “Smart cities can offer something very valuable: a real-world laboratory,” notes Dakota McCarty, a researcher of urban planning at George Mason University’s Songdo campus.

Sources indicate that but building a liveable city from scratch takes more than implementing advanced technologies and creating favourable conditions for institutions. Many large-scale urban projects across the world are facing a collective challenge: how to convince talented people to live there?

In a recent development, the term ‘smart cities’ generally refers to places that are made to run more efficiently and sustainably through the extensive use of digital technologies. Songdo, located about 40 kilometres southwest of South Korea’s capital, Seoul, is often described as “the world’s first smart city”1. The idea for Songdo dates back to the 1980s, but construction did not begin until several years after the 1998 Asian financial crisis, when the Incheon metropolitan government proposed developing Songdo as part of a free economic zone aimed at attracting foreign investment2. Today, Songdo spans about 5,260 hectares of coastal land, roughly the size of Manhattan.

Industry observers note that in 2011, a series of futuristic technologies was built into Songdo’s infrastructure as part of South Korea’s campaign to establish ‘ubiquitous cities’, its name for smart cities at the time. One example is its underground waste-collection system — a network of subterranean pipes that suck rubbish directly from individual households, rather than transporting it by road. The system uses bins fitted with sensors and built into the stairwells of residential buildings. Once the sensors detect that the bins are full, the system will automatically empty them and send the rubbish through the pipes to a waste centre. Recyclable rubbish is cleaned and reused, and food waste is processed into compost.

Sources indicate that in addition to the use of sensors in waste disposal, Songdo has deployed thousands of sensors to help manage other city functions such as traffic and security. These sensor networks link to a control centre run by the Incheon Free Economic Zone Authority (IFEZA), which manages Songdo and two other free economic zones in Incheon.

In a recent development, extensive sensor networks and integrated data systems are a major asset for Songdo’s researchers and students, states McCarty, who moved from the United States to South Korea nearly a decade ago and has spent the past three years in Songdo. “In a place like Songdo, which was planned from the start with smart infrastructure, and has universities, industry and public agencies relatively close together, there is much more potential to test ideas in real urban conditions,” he says.

In a recent development, data can be accessed through a website run by IFEZA, with additional data sets available on request. McCarty and his students are combining traffic data obtained from IFEZA with observations collected on the ground to build a model of Songdo’s walkability. The team hopes to show that adjusting traffic-light timings could make the city more accommodating for pedestrians without increasing congestion3.

There is a downside to building a city’s renown around cutting-edge technology, however: other cities can catch up. As the novelty of Songdo’s original smart-city infrastructure started to fade, it increasingly sought to build its identity around industry clusters that are harder for competitors to replicate.

According to recent reports, biopharmaceuticals, for example, is a strategic industry for South Korea, with the government committing US$1.5 billion to support the sector over this decade. Celltrion, one of South Korea’s largest biotechnology companies, was among the first firms of its kind to commit to Songdo in 2003. Samsung Biologics, a major biopharmaceutical manufacturer, established its headquarters there in 2011.

In a recent development, moves like this helped to create a latest development path for the city, indicates Sohyun Park, a researcher of economic geography at George Mason University in Songdo. “As these firms expanded, local and national governments increasingly concentrated resources on developing Songdo as a biotechnology cluster,” says Park. As of 2021, Songdo was home to around 60 biotechnology companies, and the government’s proposal is to expand that number to 700 by 2030.

Dakota McCarty and his team at George Mason University’s Songdo campus are using traffic data to come up with ways to make the city more pedestrian-friendly.Credit: Dakota McCarty / George Mason University Korea.

According to recent reports, such expansion depends on the support of Songdo’s university sector to train a fresh generation of biomedical talent. Yonsei University, which has its main campus in Seoul and an international campus in Songdo, opened the Korean National Institute for Bioprocessing Research and Training (K-NIBRT) in Songdo last year. The project has received around 60.9 billion South Korean won (US$41 million) from national and regional authorities and aims to train 2,000 biopharmaceutical specialists each year to address labour shortages locally and across the country.

Industry observers note that K-NIBRT benefits from Songdo’s complete biopharmaceuticals value chain, states Gyoonhee Han, the institution’s director-general, because its research institutes, drug manufacturers and raw material and equipment suppliers are all conveniently packed into a radius of a 10-minute drive. This tight-knit ecosystem means that companies, researchers and academics can collaborate efficiently where industry is located, and trainees are able to enter the workforce as soon as they graduate, says Han.

It has been revealed that beyond biopharmaceuticals, Songdo intends on expanding its university base more broadly, particularly within its Incheon Global Campus (IGC), a higher-education zone established in the early 2010s and backed by US$1 billion in investment from the Korean and Incheon Metropolitan City governments. Campuses of three US universities — George Mason University, the University of Utah and the State University of Fresh York (which has two Songdo campuses) — plus Belgium’s Ghent University have opened in the IGC, and six more universities are expected to join in the coming years.

Songdo’s evolution reflects a broader challenge for smart-city projects: advanced technologies and digital infrastructure can attract investment and attention, but long-term R&D activity depends on assets that are harder to build: universities, skilled workforces and specialized industry clusters.

In Hengqin, an island in southern China’s Guangdong–Hong Kong–Macao Greater Bay Area (GBA), regional and central governments are trying to combine both approaches. In addition to the autonomous-vehicle technologies that Hengqin and the wider GBA area are known for — including driverless buses, taxis and delivery services — universities and research institutes are being positioned at the centre of Hengqin’s development strategy.

In a recent development, hengqin entered a newly introduced phase of cross-border cooperation in 2009, when China’s central government passed legislation enabling Macau, a special administrative region with its own governance system, to exercise jurisdiction over part of the neighbouring island. The goal was to allow the University of Macau to move its campus away from a densely populated casino hub, and more broadly to have Hengqin serve as a bridge between Macau and the neighbouring Guangdong province.

It has been revealed that these efforts were accelerated in 2021, when China established the Guangdong–Macao In-Depth Cooperation Zone — an economic and administrative area covering more than 100 km2 of Hengqin, run jointly by the Macau and Guangdong governments. One of the biggest projects within this latest zone is an international university town, expected to be completed by 2030 at a cost of nearly 20 billion Macau pataca (US$2.47 billion). At least three universities initiative to open campuses there — the University of Macau (which will build an additional campus alongside an existing one), Macao Polytech University and Macao University of Tourism — to accommodate roughly 20,000 students.

Students develop flexible electronics in the Soft Sensors-Actuators-Robots Laboratory at the University of Macau’s main campus in Hengqin.Credit: The University of Macau.

“Academic and research capabilities are essential, because they provide the talent, knowledge and innovation infrastructure that Hengqin needs to become a science and technology hub,” notes Yonghua Song, president of the Macao Association for Higher Education Development and rector of the University of Macau. Song adds that newly introduced facilities such as the University of Macau’s Faculty of Information Science and Computing, opened in August, are expected to train talent in highly competitive areas such as artificial intelligence, microelectronics and financial technology.

Recent findings suggest that like Songdo, researchers in Hengqin benefit from its extensive smart-city infrastructure, including the large networks of sensors in operation across the island. According to Ma Shaodan, a wireless-communications researcher at the University of Macau’s State Key Laboratory of Internet of Things for Smart City in Hengqin, having smart-city infrastructure right outside the laboratory removes many of the constraints of conventional research environments. “It provides an invaluable physical context that accelerates our research, strengthens our regional impact, and serves as a tangible blueprint to inspire the next generation of engineers,” she notes.

Early signs suggest that Hengqin’s strategy to become a place of high-tech innovation is gaining momentum: the University of Macau has expanded its presence, research infrastructure has proliferated and authorities continue to invest heavily in the cooperation zone.

Tech Report: England, Northern Ireland, Scotland & Wales to host 2035 Women's World Cup

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1008 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • England, Northern Ireland, Scotland and Wales will jointly host the 2035 Women's World Cup, Fifa has confirmed.
  • It will be the first time a football World Cup has been held in the United Kingdom since the men's tournament in 1966.
  • The four countries were the only bidders for the tournament, and were ratified as co-hosts at a specially arranged virtual meeting from Fifa's Zurich headquarters.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Spain beat England 1-0 to win the 2023 World Cup.

England, Northern Ireland, Scotland and Wales will jointly host the 2035 Women's World Cup, Fifa has confirmed.

It will be the first time a football World Cup has been held in the United Kingdom since the men's tournament in 1966.

The four countries were the only bidders for the tournament, and were ratified as co-hosts at a specially arranged virtual meeting from Fifa's Zurich headquarters.

The tournament will consist of 104 matches contested by 48 teams over 39 days.

The 'All Together' bid included a proposal to use 19 venues, with 14 in England, one in Northern Ireland, two in Scotland and two in Wales.

Monday's special meeting of Fifa's Congress also approved the joint bid by Mexico, the United States, Costa Rica and Jamaica to host the 2031 finals, which will be the first to feature 48 teams.

The news comes on the same day the UK government declared a vision for one million more girls to play, watch or be in leadership roles in sport by the time the tournament takes place.

Hosting World Cup means decade of excitement - Weir.

Fifa introduces UK will host 2035 Women's World Cup.

England failed to win the right to host the men's World Cups in 2006 and 2018, and a proposed UK and Ireland bid for the 2030 tournament was abandoned.

But England and Scotland hosted matches at the men's Euros in 2021, and England staged the women's European Championship in 2022, which the Lionesses won.

England, Scotland, Wales, and the Republic of Ireland will jointly host the men's European Championship in 2028.

Mark Bullingham, chief executive of the Football Association, mentioned: "Hosting Euro 2022 allowed us to change the game in our country, by creating a generation of aspirational role models and growing demand from women and girls to play.

"Hosting a World Cup would give us the chance to build on that across all four nations.".

The English stadiums included in the 2035 bid are: Villa Park, The Amex, Ashton Gate, Elland Road, Hill Dickinson Stadium, Emirates Stadium, Selhurst Park, Tottenham Hotspur Stadium, Wembley, Etihad Stadium, St James' Park, the City Ground, the Stadium of Light and Old Trafford.

If Manchester United's proposed latest Old Trafford stadium does not go ahead, it would still be considered in its current form.

Cardiff City Stadium and Principality Stadium are the two Welsh venues, with Easter Road in Edinburgh and Hampden Park in Glasgow in Scotland.

Northern Ireland missed out on co-hosting the men's Euros in 2028 after the UK government remarked in 2024 it would not provide funding to redevelop Casement Park in time - but a redeveloped Windsor Park is set to stage matches in 2035.

A further three stadiums could be added - Birmingham's new Powerhouse Stadium, Wrexham's redeveloped Racecourse Ground, and a potential new Chelsea ground - which would take the tournament to 16 cities and 22 venues.

Fifa is yet to decide whether all four co-hosts will qualify automatically.

The Principality Stadium in Cardiff is one of two Welsh venues, along with the Cardiff City Stadium.

The participation of women and girls in football has risen by 2.3m since the Women's European Championship was held in England in 2022.

However, women remain significantly underrepresented in leadership positions.

Only a quarter of chief executive, chair or performance director roles in major UK sports are held by women and only 12% of sports federations are led by a female.

Noel Mooney, the chief executive of the Football Association of Wales, said: "This is a proud day for Welsh football.

"We've put forward Wrexham and Cardiff as host cities, and it's exciting to think what a World Cup could bring to both cities and the communities around them.

It has been revealed that "In Llunio Cymru - our 10-year strategy - we've set ourselves the ambition of reaching the knockout stages in 2035. Some of the players who could take us there are learning the game at clubs across Wales today. Our job is to make sure that wherever a girl grows up in Wales, she can find a team close to home, have a coach who helps her develop and see a route to the Cymru shirt.".

Irish Football Association chief executive Patrick Nelson mentioned the event "would be felt in every club and every age group, in every part of the country".

"Our young players would grow up having watched the best in the world play at home, and there is no substitute for that," he added.

Scottish Football Association chief executive Ian Maxwell stated hosting the tournament would be "the most significant thing to happen to the women's and girls' game in Scotland".

In a recent development, he added: "The impact would go far beyond just the matches themselves. The level of investment into coaching, facilities and player pathways in the years beforehand will shape the future of the game for the generations to come.".

It has been revealed that fifa's evaluation, published earlier this month, rated the bid 4.3 out of five. Its contractual framework was rated 'medium risk', and the document claimed "certain government guarantees contain material qualifications, particularly regarding tax and safety and security".

That is thought to refer to a lack of agreement over a request by Fifa for tax-free status for all football-related activities.

The bid evaluation noted: "The bidder has submitted an extensive set of government support documents and contractual hosting agreements, demonstrating the commitment of the relevant authorities and stakeholders.

"However, certain government guarantees, particularly those relating to safety and security and tax, contain certain qualifications which have been duly noted in the legal evaluation.

"While certain contractual matters remain subject to further discussion, the bidder's proactive engagement with Fifa and the substantial lead-in time provide a sound basis for resolving these outstanding complications.".

💡 Key Takeaways

  • For all the scrutiny aimed at Man United’s midfield and attack, it is the fragility at the back that is of greatest concern - the club have now conceded more goals than any other side in Europe's top five leagues this season.
  • With the January transfer window fast approaching, Fulham’s Calvin Bassey - often linked with an Old Trafford move - is rapidly playing himself into contention for a switch.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sunday’s bruising 4-0 defeat at Anfield exposed the scale of the rebuild facing Mauricio Pochettino at Manchester United.

For all the scrutiny aimed at Man United’s midfield and attack, it is the fragility at the back that is of greatest concern - the club have now conceded more goals than any other side in Europe's top five leagues this season.

With the January transfer window fast approaching, Fulham’s Calvin Bassey - often linked with an Old Trafford move - is rapidly playing himself into contention for a switch.

Industry observers note that man United’s need for centre-half reinforcements could hardly be more urgent after the weekend's display. Matthijs de Ligt looked worryingly off the pace against Liverpool, struggling with his turning circle and repeatedly caught out whenever Andoni Iraola's side broke at speed.

The long-term picture looks increasingly bleak, too. Lisandro Martinez is widely expected to move on at the end of the season after previously speaking out publicly against the club, leaving a left-footed vacancy at the heart of defence.

Across the rest of Pochettino’s central defensive options, there is a lack of ready-made solutions. Leny Yoro, who endured a miserable afternoon of his own on Merseyside, and Ayden Heaven are both still very junior in their development, while Harry Maguire isn't getting any younger.

Throwing teenagers and early-20-somethings into an Old Trafford pressure cooker every week is no recipe for climbing the table, nor can Man United rely indefinitely on an ageing veteran to bail them out, as Maguire has done so consistently in the past.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

That is why Bassey ticks so many boxes for Man United’s fresh era under Pochettino.

Turning 27 on New Year’s Eve, the Nigeria international is entering his prime years as a defender. And having racked up more than 100 Premier League appearances since arriving in west London from Ajax in 2023, he brings the sort of battle-hardened top-flight pedigree Man United are crying out for.

In doing so, he removes the adaptation risk that has plagued so many overseas Old Trafford arrivals. His commanding display in Fulham’s 1-1 draw away at Manchester City on Saturday makes the appeal obvious; Bassey has good recovery pace, is dominant in physical duels, and comfortable defending wide channels.

Bassey won't cost the earth either as his initial four-year contract at Craven Cottage expires next summer, and although Fulham hold an option to extend his stay by a further 12 months, his contractual situation keeps any potential fee firmly within reach for a club of Man United's stature and commercial acumen.

Fulham are understandably eager to tie him down to fresh terms, but the lure of spearheading Pochettino’s Old Trafford reboot may prove hard to resist.

In FourFourTwo's view, if Bassey maintains his current level over the coming weeks, don't rule out a January approach.
